social_history.tobacco: Former smoker, 10 pack-years, quit 15 years ago

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Language intact. Cognitive function normal.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral ptosis, left greater than right (left levator palpebrae excursion 7mm, right 10mm). Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze at 45 seconds. Limited abduction and adduction left eye — diplopia reported on leftward gaze. Pupils 3mm, equal, reactive. Facial sensation intact. Mild facial weakness bilaterally. Soft palate rises symmetrically but patient reports nasal quality to voice at end of conversation. Sternocleidomastoid strength 4/5 bilaterally.
neurological_exam.motor: Proximal upper extremity weakness: deltoids 4-/5 bilaterally. Proximal lower extremity weakness: hip flexors 4/5 bilaterally. Distal strength normal. Fatigability demonstrated — deltoid strength decreases from 4- to 3+/5 after 10 repetitions.
neurological_exam.sensory: Normal throughout. No sensory level. No paresthesias.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 2+ throughout, symmetric. Plantar responses downgoing bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Mildly slow but antalgic. No ataxia. Waddling gait pattern on prolonged walking.
neurological_exam.additional: Dysphagia reported — difficulty with solid foods. No tongue atrophy or fasciculations. Speech becomes dysarthric after prolonged speaking (fatigable dysarthria). No respiratory distress at rest. NIF -42 cmH2O (borderline; normal >-60).

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive bilateral ptosis, diplopia, and dysphagia over 4 months
patient.history_present_illness: A 52-year-old man presented to the neurology inpatient service for evaluation of progressive bilateral ptosis, diplopia, and dysphagia over 4 months. He first noticed intermittent drooping of his left eyelid approximately 4 months ago, initially occurring only in the evenings after a long day at work. He attributed this to fatigue and did not seek medical attention. Over the subsequent 6 weeks, the ptosis became bilateral, more prominent on the left, and began occurring throughout the day. He began experiencing horizontal diplopia on left lateral gaze, which worsened with sustained gaze and improved after rest. Three months ago, he started having difficulty swallowing solid foods, requiring multiple sips of water to wash down food. He denied frank aspiration but admitted to occasional coughing during meals. His wife noticed his speech became slurred and nasal after prolonged conversation, particularly in the evenings. He denied shortness of breath at rest but noted mild exertional dyspnea climbing two flights of stairs, which was new for him. There was no neck pain, no headache, no visual changes other than the diplopia, and no sensory symptoms. He had not had any recent illnesses, vaccinations, or antibiotic use. He had been seen by an ophthalmologist who excluded dry eye and structural eyelid pathology. Blood work at his primary care visit 6 weeks ago showed borderline low TSH at 0.28 (attributed to over-replacement of levothyroxine). His symptoms have a diurnal pattern — consistently worse in the afternoon and evening and better in the morning.

Abnormal decremental response consistent with neuromuscular junction disorder

findings.result: Partial repair of decrement post-exercise; decrement returns by 2-3 minutes post-exercise
findings.significance: Classic post-activation exhaustion pattern of myasthenia gravis

findings.result: Short-duration, small-amplitude polyphasic MUPs; early recruitment pattern; no spontaneous activity
findings.significance: Myopathic-pattern MUPs consistent with NMJ disorder affecting motor unit stability

findings.result: Normal motor and sensory nerve conduction velocities; normal CMAP amplitudes at rest; no demyelination
findings.significance: Excludes peripheral neuropathy and LEMS (no baseline CMAP amplitude reduction)

specialized_test.impression: Borderline-to-clearly abnormal repetitive nerve stimulation showing 9-12% decremental CMAP responses at 3 Hz in deltoid, trapezius, and nasalis muscles. Deltoid and nasalis responses exceed the 10% threshold for abnormality. Post-exercise facilitation with subsequent exhaustion pattern is characteristic of myasthenia gravis. Normal NCS argues against LEMS (LEMS shows baseline low CMAP with increment >100% at high-rate stimulation). Clinical correlation strongly supports myasthenia gravis. Single-fiber EMG recommended to increase diagnostic sensitivity.
recommended_actions: Single-fiber EMG of orbicularis oculi or extensor digitorum communis for highest sensitivity

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: Anti-AChR (Acetylcholine Receptor) Binding Antibody 0.8 nmol/L (H), Anti-AChR Blocking Antibody 18% % inhibition (H), Anti-AChR Modulating Antibody 32% % loss (H), Anti-Striated Muscle (Anti-titin) Antibody Positive qualitative (H), TSH 0.28 mIU/L (L), Anti-TPO 380 IU/mL (H).

findings.density: Soft tissue density with heterogeneous enhancement
findings.description: Rounded soft tissue mass in the anterior mediastinum anterior to the aortic arch. Lobulated contour. No calcification. No invasion of adjacent structures identified.

ct.impression: 3.1 x 2.4 cm anterior mediastinal mass with heterogeneous enhancement. In the clinical context of myasthenia gravis with positive anti-titin antibodies, this is highly suspicious for thymoma. No clear invasion of adjacent mediastinal structures on this CT but dedicated MRI chest or PET-CT may better characterize extent. Surgical evaluation for thymectomy recommended.
recommended_actions: Surgical oncology consultation for thymectomy evaluation
Consider MRI chest for better soft tissue characterization
Pathology via surgical resection preferred over biopsy for presumed thymoma

findings.significance: High blocking rate — severe NMJ transmission failure

output.impression: Markedly abnormal SFEMG of extensor digitorum communis. Increased jitter (MCD 62 us; reference <34 us) with 60% blocking rate indicates severely impaired neuromuscular junction transmission. This is the most sensitive finding for myasthenia gravis and confirms the diagnosis even with borderline serology. SFEMG sensitivity for generalized MG >95%.
recommended_actions: CT chest finding (anterior mediastinal mass) — thymectomy evaluation
Monitor respiratory function given bulbar symptoms

output.test_type: High-Rate Repetitive Nerve Stimulation (50 Hz) for LEMS differentiation

findings.significance: Fails to show pathological facilitation seen in Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS requires >100% increment)
Normal baseline CMAP — LEMS typically shows very low baseline CMAP (<2 mV in limb muscles)

output.impression: High-rate RNS does not show the >100% facilitation characteristic of Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome. Normal baseline CMAP amplitude excludes LEMS. Findings support myasthenia gravis rather than LEMS. No anti-VGCC antibody testing needed.
recommended_actions: Anti-VGCC testing not needed given normal high-rate RNS

findings.description: Lobulated anterior mediastinal mass without clear fat cleavage plane from adjacent thymus bed. No invasion of pericardium, great vessels, or pleura. No mediastinal lymphadenopathy. No pleural or pericardial effusion.

Surgical approach: VATS or median sternotomy feasible based on anatomy
output.impression: Anterior mediastinal mass 3.1 x 2.4 x 2.8 cm. Consistent with encapsulated thymoma (WHO Type A-B2 range). No radiographic invasion of adjacent structures. Resectable appearance. Recommend thoracic surgery consultation for thymectomy. Resection is both diagnostic and potentially therapeutic for associated MG.

Pre-operative optimization of MG: pyridostigmine + immunosuppression

output.proposed: Pyridostigmine 60mg every 4-6 hours for myasthenia gravis
interactions: Pyridostigmine + lisinopril: mild bradycardic additive effect with some ACE inhibitors — monitor heart rate
contraindications: Avoid aminoglycosides — worsen NMJ blockade in MG
Avoid fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) — worsen NMJ in MG
Avoid certain antiarrhythmics (procainamide, quinidine) — NMJ blockade

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Myasthenia gravis, generalized (MGFA Class IIb — moderate bulbar involvement), AChR-antibody positive with thymoma

differential.key_features: LEMS shows baseline low CMAP with >100% increment at 50Hz RNS; proximal limb weakness without prominent ocular findings; anti-VGCC positive; high-rate RNS normal in this patient; anti-VGCC negative
TSH suppressed initially but free T4 normal, anti-TPO positive (Hashimoto); no proptosis; no lid retraction; fatigable pattern inconsistent with restrictive myopathy of Graves orbitopathy
CPEO has symmetric ophthalmoplegia without true fatigability pattern; EMG would show myopathic features; anti-AChR negative; bulbar symptoms atypical for CPEO
No MRI abnormality; multiple cranial nerve involvement and fatigability inconsistent with single brainstem lesion; sensory intact; no other brainstem signs

critical_actions: Serial FVC and NIF monitoring every 4-6 hours (borderline respiratory function with bulbar involvement — crisis risk)
CT chest to identify thymoma (present in 15% of MG)
SFEMG for definitive diagnosis when serology equivocal
Initiate pyridostigmine after ruling out cholinergic crisis
Surgical referral for thymectomy (thymoma requires resection; thymectomy also beneficial for non-thymoma MG)
Avoid aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, procainamide — NMJ blocking agents
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT use aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin) — worsens NMJ blockade
Do NOT use fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin) — worsen MG
Do NOT initiate corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization — risk of transient worsening precipitating crisis
Do NOT attribute borderline RNS to normal — clinical context (fatigability, ptosis, diplopia, dysarthria) is crucial
Do NOT delay thymectomy evaluation with confirmed anterior mediastinal mass
key_reasoning_points: Borderline AChR antibody titer (0.8 nmol/L) with clearly abnormal blocking and modulating antibodies supports MG even without a clearly elevated binding antibody
Positive anti-titin antibodies in a 52-year-old man with MG strongly predict thymoma — CT chest mandatory
SFEMG is the most sensitive test for MG (>95%) and should be ordered when serology is equivocal
Concurrent Hashimoto thyroiditis is consistent with polyautoimmunity seen in MG patients
Borderline NIF (-42 cmH2O) and FVC (72% predicted) with bulbar symptoms warrants inpatient monitoring for myasthenic crisis
Fatigable ptosis and diplopia with diurnal variation (worse evening) is classic MG; thyroid ophthalmopathy causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmopathy
Thymectomy improves long-term outcomes in MG even in non-thymoma patients (MGTX trial evidence)

red_herrings.intended_effect: Clinician may attribute ptosis and weakness to thyroid disease (hyperthyroidism or Graves ophthalmopathy)
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Free T4 normal; anti-TPO elevated (Hashimoto, not Graves); no proptosis; fatigable pattern inconsistent with thyroid ophthalmopathy; TSH suppression is mild over-replacement — reduce levothyroxine dose, but this is not the cause of MG symptoms

red_herrings.data_point: RNS decrement of only 9% in trapezius (below 10% threshold)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Clinician may dismiss borderline RNS and delay SFEMG, leading to missed MG diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: 10% decrement threshold is a statistical convention; deltoid shows 11% and nasalis shows 12% — clearly abnormal; clinical fatigability pattern mandates SFEMG regardless of borderline RNS
